# Diagnosing PT Cruiser Overheating and Fan Failure

A PT Cruiser bubbling coolant from the reservoir while the temperature gauge reads normal is a classic symptom of a specific thermodynamic failure: the cooling fan is not engaging, causing air temperature to rise faster than liquid can dissipate heat. Even though you replaced the thermostat, the core issue remains active because the system lacks active airflow when the vehicle stops or at low speeds. The fact that bubbles appear only when hot suggests the coolant is boiling due to insufficient heat exchange, rather than a leak in the radiator itself.

The immediate red flag is the non-functional fan. You mentioned checking the under-hood fuse and finding it intact, yet replaced the interior fuse with no success. This discrepancy points toward a failure downstream of the power source, likely within the relay circuit or the fan module itself. In many PT Cruisers, the cooling fans are controlled by a dedicated relay located in the main junction box, often near the battery. If the fuse is good but the fan doesn't spin, the relay contacts may be pitted or the control logic from the Engine Control Module (ECM) has failed to send the ground signal required to activate the circuit.

To isolate the fault without a multimeter at hand, you can perform a direct power test. Disconnect the connector from the fan motor and probe the wires directly with a battery lead. If the fans spin vigorously when powered directly by the battery, the issue is definitely electrical control (bad relay or ECM signal). If they don't spin, the motor has failed internally, likely due to burnt windings from prolonged overheating cycles. Replacing the motor in this scenario is often cheaper than repairing the complex wiring harness behind the grille.

Once you confirm the fan works with direct power, the focus shifts to the relay. Locate the cooling fan relay in the under-dash or engine bay fuse block. Swap it with a known-good relay of the same type, such as the horn or A/C compressor relay if they share the same part number. If the fan engages, replace the original relay. This is a low-cost fix that resolves many "noisy" overheating complaints where the ECM is trying to command the fan but getting no response from a stuck relay.

If the relay and motor are functional, investigate the thermal switch located near the radiator. Unlike the engine thermostat which controls liquid flow, this switch detects coolant temperature directly at the radiator outlet. If it fails open, the ECM never receives the signal to trigger the fan. This is a common failure point in PT Cruisers; the switch can stick or corrode internally despite the reservoir bubbling normally when cold.

Another possibility involves the wiring harness connector behind the grille. These plastic connectors are notorious for developing hairline cracks due to heat cycling and vibration. Inspect the pins for corrosion or green oxidation, which increases resistance enough to prevent the high-current fan from drawing sufficient amps. Clean any corrosion with contact cleaner and ensure the locking tabs on the connector are seated flush against the housing.

Finally, consider the possibility of a faulty radiator cap. If the system pressure drops below 13.5 PSI (the standard rating), the coolant boils at a lower temperature, causing vigorous bubbling even when the engine isn't critically hot. While this explains the overflow, it doesn't explain the fan failure. Addressing the fan first is critical; driving with a non-functioning fan and a compromised cap will almost certainly lead to head gasket failure within days.
